This is a review of a task, not the task itself. Do not do the clinical work. You have only read tools: there is no write tool and no finish tool.

Below is the instruction an agent receives for task discharge-medrec. Read it, then use the read tools to read everything it depends on: the clinic policies it names or that govern it (read_policy), the patients, orders, results, notes and inbox items it points at, and your own context (get_context).

Report every ambiguity you find, where a careful clinician could not tell what the task wants:
- two_readings: a sentence of the instruction or a policy reads two ways, and the two readings lead to different actions;
- missing_fact: a fact the work needs (a date, a dose, a threshold, a recipient, a patient) is not in the instruction, the policies or the chart;
- conflict: two sources (the instruction, a policy, a note, an order, a result) say different things about the same point.

Quote the exact words each finding rests on. Leave out what is only hard, long or clinically unusual but has one reading. If you find none, say so with an empty list.

End with one final message that holds only this JSON object, with no text before or after it:
{"findings": [{"kind": "two_readings" | "missing_fact" | "conflict", "source": "<instruction, or the policy id, or the resource as Type/id>", "quote": "<the exact words>", "readings": ["<what one reading asks the agent to do>", "<what another asks>"], "explanation": "<why a careful clinician could not tell which is meant>"}]}
Give readings two or more entries for two_readings and conflict, and none for missing_fact.

The instruction for discharge-medrec:

<instruction>
Walter Kim was discharged from St. Brigid on Monday (10/19). Please reconcile his outpatient medication list per RBC-TOC-02 and flag anything you can't resolve to me.

— Dr. Okafor

</instruction>

content.source: Clinic-local reconciliation rules (design section 4, T4), consistent with The Joint Commission National Patient Safety Goal NPSG.03.06.01 'Maintain and communicate accurate patient medication information' (Ambulatory Health Care NPSGs effective January 2026: compare the patient's medication information with the medications ordered and resolve discrepancies such as omissions, duplications and changes; summarized from the 2026 ambulatory NPSG document, not quoted verbatim). The rules themselves are local and not verified against an external text.
content.text:
RBC-TOC-02 Medication reconciliation after hospital discharge

Applies when a patient returns from a hospital stay and the outpatient medication list must match the discharge documentation before the post-discharge visit.

§1 Sources
Reconcile against the discharge documentation of the hospital stay that just ended. The latest signed addendum supersedes the discharge summary where they differ.

§2 Conditional instructions
Act on a conditional instruction when results already in the chart satisfy its condition. Otherwise create a Task due when the result is expected.

§3 Formulary substitutions
An inpatient formulary substitution marked as such reverts to the home drug: keep the home drug and do not order the substitute.

§4 Aliases
An alias or brand name for an existing order (for example a brand name, or a release-form abbreviation such as "ER", for the same drug and dose) means no change.

§5 Home medications not addressed
A home medication the discharge documentation does not address must not be changed: message the PCP, with the medication order in the message's about.

§6 Making changes
Change a dose by modifying the existing order (stop it and replace it); resume a held order rather than duplicating it. Document the reconciliation in a progress note: each change and the document it comes from, citing the documents and results relied on.

St. Brigid Regional - Discharge Summary
Patient: Walter Kim   DOB 1952-02-19
Admitted 2026-10-14, discharged 2026-10-19. Service: Hospital Medicine.

Principal diagnosis: acute on chronic systolic heart failure.
Other diagnoses: acute kidney injury; coronary artery disease; hyperlipidemia.

Hospital course: admitted with dyspnea and 4 kg weight gain. Diuresed with IV furosemide. Creatinine rose to 1.9 mg/dL on 10/16 with diuresis and lisinopril, and lisinopril was held. Euvolemic at discharge.

Discharge medications:
- Furosemide 40 mg by mouth daily (increased from 20 mg).
- Metoprolol XL 50 mg by mouth daily: continue.
- Atorvastatin 40 mg by mouth nightly: continue.
- Aspirin 81 mg by mouth daily: continue.
- Lisinopril: held for AKI. Resume home 10 mg daily when SCr < 1.5 on post-discharge labs.
- Spironolactone 12.5 mg by mouth daily: start.
- Potassium chloride: stop.
- Pantoprazole 40 mg by mouth daily (formulary substitution for home omeprazole).

Follow-up: Riverbend Family Medicine within 7 days; basic metabolic panel 2 days after discharge and 1 week after starting spironolactone.

Samuel Boateng, MD

Discharge medications:

- Aspirin 81 mg by mouth daily: continue.
- Omeprazole 20 mg by mouth daily: continue.

Follow-up: Riverbend Family Medicine within 7 days; echocardiogram in 3 months.

Samuel Boateng, MD
